title: Email, SMS, voice, web: one story, many doors
body_md:
## The bell doesn’t vouch for the visitor

Your phone buzzes at 7:40 with a text from your bank about a card payment you don’t recognize. Before you’ve finished reading, it rings: the bank’s fraud desk, calm and well informed, already aware of the text. It would be quicker, the caller says, to sort this out on the phone than in the app. Nothing in the call is clumsy. What is wrong is that two channels now vouch for each other, and one person stands behind both.

A channel is a doorbell. It tells you someone is at the door and nothing about who. An attack vector is the route a request takes to reach you: email carries links and attachments, a text or chat message delivers a short instruction, a phone call leans on you in real time, and a search, an ad or a QR code puts a page in your path. The same story hops from one to the next, and each hop borrows credibility from the last. Don’t rank the channels by open-rate figures nobody can source, and don’t assume phone scams are rare because they take more effort. What matters is the action being asked of you.

### Three questions at every hand-off

Ask: **Who is making this claim? What do they want me to open, share, install, approve or pay? Where did this address or number come from?** A familiar sender name, a caller ID, a logo, a high spot in the search results: each is something the sender can arrange, and none is an identity check. HTTPS protects the connection to a site, but it doesn’t show that the site belongs to the organization you had in mind. And genuine alerts do arrive by text and email, so deleting every unexpected message is no answer when one describes a real problem with your account.

A safe check starts outside the incoming message. Open the service’s app on your device, type an address you know, or call the number on a statement or in your own contacts. Then look at the account, or ask the organization whether such a request exists. If the request concerns a colleague, use the work directory you already had and the usual approval route. Switching from the email to the phone number printed in that email proves nothing, because the number rings in the same house the email was written in. The sender supplied both routes.

### What no channel can promise

Email authentication and spam filters cut down some spoofing, yet a hijacked genuine mailbox can still send something harmful. A text thread can seat a spoofed message among real ones. A caller may already know your name and the details of your account. Search results and ads lead to real services and fake ones alike. Reading the URL helps, but a familiar domain can host a compromised page, and a phone screen hides part of the address. No visual clue replaces looking at the transaction inside a service you trust.

**The routine:** pause when a request would hand someone control, leave the channel it came in on, check through a source you chose earlier, and act through the normal service only if it confirms. If you have already entered data or paid, contact the provider promptly; what comes next depends on what was exposed.

widget_config.goal: Work out what a message, call or page wants you to do, then check it by a route you chose yourself.
widget_config.today_action: Pick one service that matters to you and save its official app or support contact now, so you have something to call back on later.
widget_config.scope: General principles about channels and verification; the NCSC’s reporting instructions apply to the UK. The examples are invented. Which channel a message used, or how polished it looks, proves neither fraud nor safety on its own.

sources.title: NCSC: How to spot a scam email, text message or call
sources.scope: UK consumer guidance, published 2021 and reviewed 2022; the habit of checking independently applies anywhere.

sources.title: FTC: What to do if you were scammed
sources.scope: US consumer guidance sorted by what was exposed or paid, as of June 2026; your local rights may differ.

blocks.title: A parcel text, then a friendly call
blocks.situation: A text says a parcel needs its address corrected at `https://parcel-help.example`. Twenty minutes later a caller assures you the link is safe and asks for a card number to pay a tiny fee.
blocks.analysis: The caller and the link are propping up the same unverified claim. A customs or delivery fee is possible, so the fee alone proves nothing either way. Look up the real order, or open the courier’s own app, and ignore both the link and the callback number the text gave you.

blocks.title: A library email you can check
blocks.situation: Your library emails to say a book you reserved is ready, with the last day you can collect it. The message carries the library’s name and a link, but asks for no payment and no password.
blocks.analysis: This may well be genuine. Open the library’s app or its usual website and look at the reservation there. Checking costs a minute: you won’t miss your book, and you won’t have to trust a link you can’t vouch for.

blocks.title: Follow one claim across channels
blocks.setup: An invented storage-service warning reaches you while you’re traveling. Follow the same claim as it moves from email to phone call to web search.

steps.prompt: An email says your files will be deleted tonight and offers a “restore” link. What do you do first?

choices.text: Open your usual storage app and look for notices there.
choices.consequence: You see the state of the account without touching the email’s link.
choices.explanation: Urgency is a reason to check, not to comply on the spot.

choices.text: Click the restore link; the email does use your name.
choices.consequence: The link, not you, decides where you land.
choices.explanation: A scammer can know your name before ever writing to you.

steps.prompt: Then someone calls, says they are from support and tells you to dial the number printed in the email. How do you check?

choices.text: Call the number printed in the email.
choices.consequence: The same person may pick up.
choices.explanation: Making the call yourself changes nothing when the contact details came from the party you are checking.

choices.text: Hang up and find support’s number in your own app or saved records.
choices.consequence: Your new route doesn’t pass through the caller.
choices.explanation: A number supplied by the claim itself is not independent.

steps.prompt: A web search shows a sponsored “storage recovery” result. Which way do you go?

choices.text: Skip it and use the app or an address you already know.
choices.consequence: You land where you meant to go, not where an ad slot pointed you.
choices.explanation: A search result is a path to a page, not proof of whose page it is.

choices.consequence: You may type your password into a page that has nothing to do with the service.

steps.prompt: The official app shows your files untouched and no warning. What now?

choices.text: Follow the email anyway, in case the app is running behind.
choices.consequence: The original claim takes control again.
choices.explanation: A mismatch is a reason to contact support by a route you know, not to go back to the suspicious link.

choices.text: Treat the incoming claims as unconfirmed, and report or block them through the provider’s usual route.
choices.consequence: The chain ends here, and your real account stays as it was.
choices.explanation: What the trusted app shows outweighs what the incoming messages say.

blocks.debrief: Run the hops again: the email, the caller and the ad can all tell one story. A check is independent only when the address or contact comes from a source you had before the story began.

questions.prompt: A real bank text warns of unusual activity. What is the safest way to deal with it?

choices.text: Ignore every text, since banks never send alerts.
choices.explanation: Real services do send alerts, so check independently instead of dismissing them.

choices.text: Open the bank app you already use and review activity, or reach support from there.
choices.explanation: That answers a genuine alert without leaning on the message’s link.

questions.prompt: Your caller ID shows your clinic’s name. What does that prove?

choices.text: Only what the phone displayed. Call back on a number you know for the clinic before sharing anything.
choices.explanation: A displayed name can be set by the caller, so it says little about who is calling.

choices.text: That the caller is the clinic.
choices.explanation: A name on a screen is not proof of identity.

questions.prompt: An email and the page its link opens show the same logo. Which conclusion is sound?

choices.text: Matching logos prove the page is official.
Both may belong to the same sender, so check through a separate source.
choices.explanation: Two things supplied by the same unknown sender agreeing with each other is weak evidence.

questions.prompt: Why does an HTTPS page not show that an offer is legitimate?

choices.text: HTTPS protects the connection to the page, not the truth of what it says.
choices.explanation: A scam site can use HTTPS too.
It does encrypt traffic. Whether the business is who it claims to be is a separate question.
